concepts.name: Lateral movement
concepts.summary: Lateral movement is the phase of an intrusion where an adversary moves from an initially compromised host to other systems in the environment, hunting for higher-value access — domain controllers, file servers, admin workstations, cloud control planes. It usually combines harvested credentials (hashes, tickets, tokens, cached passwords) with legitimate remote-access mechanisms: SMB and admin shares, RDP, WinRM/PowerShell remoting, SSH, WMI, or remote service creation. Because the traffic rides protocols administrators use daily, detection is about context rather than mechanism: authentication patterns that don't match a user's history, one account fanning out to many hosts in a short window, workstation-to-workstation logons, and remote-execution artifacts appearing on machines with no admin-change ticket.

concepts.name: Command and control (C2)
concepts.summary: Command and control (C2) is the channel an adversary maintains with compromised systems to issue tasking, stage tooling, and exfiltrate data. Modern C2 hides in allowed egress: HTTPS to attacker infrastructure or abused cloud services, DNS tunneling, and legitimate platforms (chat services, code-hosting, file-sharing) repurposed as relays. Implants typically beacon — short, periodic check-ins with jitter — rather than holding connections open. Defensive signals include periodicity analysis of outbound flows, rare or newly registered destination domains, TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA4) anomalies, unusually long DNS labels or high-entropy subdomains, and processes generating network traffic that have no business doing so. Blocking known infrastructure helps but decays fast; behavioral beacon detection ages better.

concepts.name: Living off the land (LOLBins)
concepts.summary: Living off the land is the practice of conducting an intrusion using tools already present on the target — signed OS binaries, admin utilities, and scripting engines — instead of custom malware. The binaries involved are called LOLBins: certutil downloading payloads, mshta or rundll32 executing script and DLL payloads, bitsadmin fetching files, regsvr32 pulling scriptlets, wmic for remote execution. The appeal is evasion: the executables are signed, whitelisted, and routine, so file-reputation and simple allowlisting see nothing new. Detection shifts to arguments and context — the pairing of binary, command line, parent process, and network destination. A signed binary in an unusual role (certutil with a URL, rundll32 with no arguments, an office parent) is the signal, not the binary itself.
